title: Represent Numbers in Different Ways

sourceTextSkillAdaptation.prompt: In the original warm-up,what three-digit number equals 300+60+10? Explain how the two tens terms combine,and distinguish this sum from standard expanded form.

originalSourceHeadings.heading: Warm-up: Which One Doesn't Belong: Numbers within 1,000 (10 minutes)
Activity 1: Card Sort: Numbers in Their Different Forms (15 minutes)
Activity 2: Numbers in Different Forms Round Table (20 minutes)
Cool-down: Let Me Count the Ways (5 minutes)

learnerSourceCheck.prompt: In the original warm-up,what three-digit number equals 300+60+10? Explain how the two tens terms combine,and distinguish this sum from standard expanded form.

supplementalLessonTeachingGuidance.sourceGoal: Let’s represent numbers in different ways.
supplementalLessonTeachingGuidance.sourceLearningGoals: Represent numbers to 1,000 in different ways using place value understanding.
teachingSteps: Compare the four warm-up representations and justify a choice.
Distinguish standard expanded form from other correct decompositions.
Match all twelve cards by place-value value and explain with a partner.
Pass the four-box sheet right,keeping the same original number and recording different decompositions.
Explain exchanges and patterns,then use the new Cool-down to represent a different whole.
supplementalLessonTeachingGuidance.caution: Do not force one WODB choice,one decomposition or equal-sized match groups. Preserve the whole during exchanges; standard expanded form has a specific digit-value meaning.
supplementalLessonTeachingGuidance.targetRichV2Field: guarded canonical English teaching replacement CommonCoreG3Unit3Lesson1RichV2

firstPartyPractice.prompt: Write 600+20+5 as a numeral,then give its word name and a different decomposition. Enter the numeral; your teacher reviews the additional representations.

independentEdulyticsCoolDown.prompt: New Edulytics task: represent 572 as counts of hundreds,tens and ones. Enter ONE grouping as three non-negative whole numbers in hundreds,tens,ones order,separated by commas. Then show two different decompositions and explain an exchange that keeps the whole unchanged. Counts of tens or ones may exceed 9; your teacher reviews distinctness and the extra forms.

stageC.humanRubric: Original source deckA–L has five groups:A–G–L=175,B–H=813,C–F=371,D–I–J=299,E–K=329. CardC diagram 3 hundreds 7 tens 1 one;J 2 hundreds 9 tens 9 ones. Standard expanded form is distinct from other correct sums. For round table,check one original three-digit whole,three different decompositions,each pass right and final return,connections and actual discussion. The numeric hundreds,tens,ones checker accepts equivalent non-standard exchanges and checks one grouping only; teacher reviews word form,diagrams,other decompositions,distinctness and authorship. Publisher card/round-table PDFs were inspected; artwork is not copied.

matchingScope: Hundreds,tens,ones counts checked by exact100h+10t+o=target,non-negative counts0..1000,target1..1000. Non-standard counts over9 intentionally accepted. Numeric anchor validates one grouping only; other forms, distinct boxes, card matching and actual passing/dialogue require teacher review.
